title: Transfer 'shark' De Zerbi hopes to drag Spurs up from depths
description: Through his self-confessed love of the transfer window, Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi hopes he can guide his club back up the Premier League table.
fullText:
There was a moment last season when Roberto de Zerbi turned to his Tottenham players and asked: "Did we pass away?"

The scenes after his first game in charge - a 1-0 defeat at Sunderland - painted a grim picture.

In the dressing room, De Zerbi said players were lying on their backs, some crying following the loss at the Stadium of Light.

It was the first of seven matches De Zerbi had to keep Spurs in the Premier League.

While survival was only secured on the final day, the 47-year-old now believes he can help the club rise from the ignominy of a turbulent 2025-26 campaign.

Four months on from the broken dressing room in Sunderland, the contrast is stark.

At the team's hotel in Sydney for their pre-season tour, just a stone's throw from the Harbour Bridge and iconic Opera House, De Zerbi's players are laughing, smiling and enjoying coffees made by their own barista on a private floor.

Competitive table tennis matches are taking place as a club-record £237m worth of new signings integrate into a squad dreaming of a return to the upper echelons of English football and a renewed challenge for trophies.

Club-record signing Sandro Tonali, plus new arrivals Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke, Andrew Robertson and Martin Dubravka have all featured on Spurs' pre-season tour.

After featuring for Argentina in the World Cup final, Marcos Senesi was granted extended leave and is the only new recruit not to have featured in Australia and New Zealand, but has now begun training at Hotspur Way.

"I deserve to want the top players, because now Tottenham deserves to build up a top team," De Zerbi said.

It was an unusual position for Spurs, but they had two transfer plans: one for relegation and one for survival.

De Zerbi, who reiterates he would have continued managing Spurs in the Championship, is happy to be working from Plan A, including "respecting the will" of players such as club captain Cristian Romero and goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario, who could yet leave.

"At the beginning of my time in April I had one million individual meetings," he jokes. "They told me if they didn't want to be here. I said: 'Yes, help me to stay up, and then I help you to leave.

"'If you don't help me to stay up, you stay underwater with me'."

Spurs have undergone radical change over the past 12 months amid understandable fan anger, with new chief executive Vinai Venkatesham leading the organisation on behalf of the Lewis Family Trust.

Venkatesham, alongside technical director Johan Lange, is leading negotiations. Lange is the only senior figure from the previous regime to remain in post.

They are supported by director of football operations Rafi Moersen and new performance director Dan Lewindon, both of whom arrived from Manchester City's parent company, City Football Group.

Lewindon has been tasked with improving Spurs' injury record.

But De Zerbi is hands on in all areas of the club and says "in the transfer market, when I want one player, I become like a shark.

That approach has helped secure record deals for £85m Fernandes from West Ham and £100m Tonali from Newcastle.

"I love working in the transfer market. It's not a pressure, it's one of the nicest parts in my work, in my job," he explained.

But where does that enjoyment come from?

"I don't know, maybe because when you take the decision, you take the responsibility. If the coach calls the player, you can build a special connection at the beginning.

"With Mateus Fernandes, I spoke with the mum, with the father."

De Zerbi told Fernandes' father that he would be his "second dad" and look after him in England.

Spurs also signed defender Van Hecke despite reported interest from Chelsea, having already beaten Manchester United and Manchester City to the two record-breaking midfielders.

Transfers are a world of game theory. Insiders have told BBC Sport that Spurs knew they had to be both aggressive and quick, with the first quality likely extending to fees, wages and De Zerbi's personal involvement in courting players.

After the 2-2 draw with Brighton in April, in which Georginio Rutter scored a 95th-minute equaliser to dent Spurs' survival hopes, De Zerbi revealed he messaged Van Hecke, who assisted the goal.

"You wanted to push down Tottenham for Brighton when you made the assist to Rutter, now you have to come to me, you have no choice," De Zerbi revealed.

For Tonali, De Zerbi detailed how he texted him the day after Spurs secured their Premier League status with a final-day win over Everton, before meeting him at his home in Brescia in what proved to be a decisive conversation.

Club staff then completed the deal following several further discussions.

Now he is teasing what he calls a final attacking "bomba", with moves for two forwards expected, including one for Manchester City's Savinho.

De Zerbi believes it would be wrong to suggest Spurs are spending irresponsibly.

He said he is under "no pressure" despite the Lewis family injecting £100m into the club in June because it was desperately needed, arguing that Chelsea, Arsenal and Liverpool have all done the same in recent years.

There have also been departures, with the club earning substantial fee for Luka Vuskovic's £45m move to Brighton. Doubts remain over the futures of midfielder Lucas Bergvall and England full-back Djed Spence.

"We assessed the request of Vuskovic [to join Brighton], with Vinai, with Johan together, because I consider Tottenham's money my money," De Zerbi said.

"It's like the owner is my father, I think you don't want to ask your father to lose money.

"Like all the big clubs, we have to sell a player at as big of a price [as possible] and we have to bring a player with a small price, we are starting for a plan of five seasons because we are building."

There was also the disciplined decision not to sign Joao Palhinha on a permanent transfer from Bayern Munich, not because De Zerbi felt he was not good enough, but because the overall financial package was not considered suitable.

After the Sunderland game, there was also a sense of sadness and negativity among staff at the training ground.

"The day after I organised a meeting without players and I said, 'The first one I see say something negative, I send you home immediately'," said De Zerbi.

It is now about changing the "behaviour, attitude and spirit" of those at Spurs who suffered that traumatic season, having also finished 17th the previous campaign, albeit without the same fear of relegation and with a Europa League triumph under Ange Postecoglou.

He explains that he took his players for "one big dinner in Mayfair, with alcohol" and believes Spurs were unfortunate in their final matches and could have secured survival sooner.

"I think they considered themselves in that moment worse than the people thought," De Zerbi admits, adding that the healing process continues. "I hope next time they organise [dinner and drinks] for themselves.

"With love, friendship and care, you become top, top, top."

title: Why Arsenal are signing Newcastle captain Guimaraes
description: With Bruno Guimaraes set to sign for Premier League champions Arsenal, BBC Sport look at why the Gunners wanted the Newcastle skipper.
fullText:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta made clear in the immediate aftermath of the Gunners' Premier League title win that they would need to be ambitious to build on their success - and the club have backed him with the move to sign Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes.

Arsenal won the league for the first time in 22 years last season and reached the Champions League final where they were beaten by Paris St-Germain.

But as soon as the curtain came down on that campaign and the parade to celebrate their new silverware had finished, Arteta's thoughts moved to taking Arsenal to a "different dimension".

And with Brazil's Guimaraes set to be part of a new-look Arsenal midfield, the club believe they are signing a player who will do exactly that.

Arteta has always been keen on signing players with Premier League experience and who have shown they can operate with the demands at the highest level.

And with the addition of the 28-year-old, the club's aim of creating one of the best midfields in world football is a step closer.

There are a number of reasons why Guimaraes was the player Arteta decided can ensure Arsenal are ready to fight on multiple fronts.

The Gunners were plagued with injuries last season and, despite a £250m spend in the last summer transfer window, a player's robustness has always been considered when making signings.

Arsenal played 63 games in all competitions last season and have revamped their medical department before the new campaign.

Christian Norgaard, who is set to move to Everton, was brought in last summer but was not trusted by Arteta and was limited to just seven appearances and one start in the league last season.

That put heavy demands on Martin Zubimendi and Declan Rice, with the former dropping out of the side completely as the amount of work he was asked to do took its toll during the run-in.

Rice is coming back from a World Cup campaign where he helped England reach the semi-finals after a season in which he played the most minutes of any outfield player at Arsenal.

Rice has been carrying a hamstring issue but rest is expected to have helped to ease the problem, with Guimaraes' addition ensuring there will be no dip in quality if Arteta rotates his starting XI, while the ceiling of the midfield is raised too.

Arteta is known for demanding intensity in training and with Guimaraes set to join a midfield stocked with Rice, Zubimendi, captain Martin Odegaard, Eberechi Eze, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Ethan Nwaneri, there will be no shortage of competition.

Arsenal have a leadership group that supports club captain Odegaard but, with the addition of Guimaraes, they will be bringing in a player who is a natural leader.

Guimaraes became Newcastle's talisman during his time at St James' Park and, as Arteta looks to maximise every marginal gain he can, the Brazilian's ability and his way of connecting with supporters will be another weapon.

Arsenal have had campaigns seriously affected by injury, but Guimaraes has missed just 16 Premier League games since he signed for Newcastle in 2022.

And his impact is backed up by the fact Newcastle's win percentage (12.5%), points per game (0.7), average goals for (0.8) and even average goals against (1.6) all suffer in the top flight when he is not available.

Although it is an admittedly larger sample size, Opta data shows that Newcastle's win percentage (50.7%), points per game (1.7), average goals for (1.9) and average goals against (1.3) have been significantly higher when Guimaraes has featured.

Guimaraes was Newcastle's top scorer in the league last season with nine goals and he provided four assists for Brazil at the World Cup in his five starts.

Despite missing six games with hamstring injury towards the end of last season, Guimaraes still ranked in the top five players across the league for defensive line-breaking passes (46) and through balls (21).

The Reds' number 18 had already been the subject of a rumoured exit from Anfield earlier in the summer, although Lewis Steele hinted in July that he'd be 'surprised' if the Netherlands international were to leave this month.

According to Simon Jones for the Daily Mail, Liverpool have no plans to sell Gakpo this summer, despite Spurs making their interest known, with Merseyside chiefs keen to enhance rather than curtail their options in attack.

Between the Dutchman's age (27) and contract status (four years remaining on his current deal), and the rising market prices for players of his high-level experience, it'd require a gargantuan offer for LFC to alter their stance on the forward, who they signed from PSV Eindhoven for £44m midway through the 2022/23 season.

title: Record number of new managers for season like no other
description: The 2026-27 Premier League season has not yet kicked off, but it has already made history for its managerial changes.
fullText:
The 2026-27 Premier League season has not yet kicked off, but it has already made history.

Nine clubs are set to begin the campaign with a new permanent manager - the highest number ever for the top flight's opening weekend.

From Liverpool and Manchester City to Newcastle United and Chelsea, change has swept across almost half the league.

Four pointers to most open Premier League title race in years

The scale of turnover has dramatically reshaped the Premier League's managerial landscape.

Liverpool appointed Andoni Iraola after Arne Slot was sacked, while Manchester City turned to Enzo Maresca following Pep Guardiola's resignation after a trophy-laden spell at Etihad Stadium.

Chelsea turned to Xabi Alonso after Liam Rosenior's ill-fated term came to an end, Bournemouth appointed Marco Rose after Andoni Iraola's contract expired, and Nottingham Forest hired Oliver Glasner following Vitor Pereira's dismissal.

Crystal Palace turned to Pierre Sage after Glasner left at the end of his contract, Fulham appointed Alvaro Arbeloa after Marco Silva's deal expired, while Ipswich Town named Gary O'Neil as successor when Kieran McKenna resigned.

Newcastle United are also expected to appoint Matthias Jaissle after Eddie Howe stepped down, taking the total to nine clubs beginning the season with a new permanent boss.

The previous record came in 2016-17, when eight clubs began the campaign under new management.

That summer included Guardiola's arrival at Manchester City and Antonio Conte's appointment at Chelsea, with the Italian going on to win the title in his first season.

Before that, seven clubs changed manager before the 1995-96 season, while six did so in 2012-13.

Alonso heals Real Madrid scars to lead Chelsea's senior revolution

Top players, title fights - why Iraola feels ready for Liverpool

Arsenal's Mikel Arteta, appointed in December 2019, is now the league's longest-serving manager despite having been in charge for less than seven years.

Only Atletico Madrid's Diego Simeone, who has led the Spanish side since December 2011, has been in charge of a club for longer across Europe's five major leagues.

Closer to home, Aston Villa's Unai Emery and Leeds United's Daniel Farke have been with their current clubs for more than three seasons, while Sunderland boss Regis le Bris, appointed in July 2024, is already the fourth longest-serving manager in the division.

Manchester United boss Michael Carrick illustrates just how quickly things have changed. Although he became the club's permanent manager in May after taking interim charge in January, only 10 Premier League managers have been in post longer than him.

Carrick is also United's seventh permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Tottenham Hotspur's Roberto de Zerbi, appointed in March, is only one place further back.

New boss Maresca is perfect for Man City - Gvardiol

Another sub-plot this season will be whether the traditional 'new manager bounce' still exists.

The theory suggests teams often enjoy a short-term improvement after appointing a new head coach, helped by renewed motivation, tactical tweaks and a psychological reset.

This season the concept could be tested like never before. Matchweek one is expected to feature three fixtures between clubs led by new managers - Fulham against Chelsea, Manchester City versus Bournemouth, and Liverpool travelling to Newcastle - with each of those teams adapting to new tactical ideas and coaching methods simultaneously.

Liverpool's start is particularly unusual. Iraola's first six Premier League matches will all come against teams under new permanent managers, with Forest, Ipswich, Fulham, Bournemouth and Manchester City following Newcastle.

For the first time since 1985-86, England's top flight will begin without Sir Alex Ferguson, Arsene Wenger, Jose Mourinho, Jurgen Klopp or Guardiola occupying a dugout.

Between them, they have won 26 of the league's 34 titles.

More than that, they defined successive generations of English football. Ferguson's relentless United sides set the standard during the Premier League's formative years before Wenger transformed perceptions of preparation, sports science and nutrition at Arsenal.

Mourinho introduced a new level of tactical pragmatism and psychological warfare, Klopp's high-intensity pressing reshaped Liverpool, and Guardiola's positional football established one of the most dominant teams in English football history.

Only Ferguson, Mourinho and Guardiola have successfully defended a Premier League title, a feat Arteta now has the chance to emulate after leading the Gunners to the championship last season.

His traditional rivals all begin the campaign under new managers, while Carrick starts his first full season as the Red Devils head coach.

Time will tell if the next defining figure emerges immediately. But with the managers who shaped more than three decades of Premier League history now gone, the 2026-27 season marks the beginning of a new chapter.

The upheaval did not begin this summer. The 2025-26 Premier League season featured 11 managerial changes, with Forest among the clubs to make multiple appointments during the campaign.

The average tenure of a top-flight boss now stands at about 20 months, illustrating just how fleeting life in one of football's most demanding jobs can now be.

Recent history also suggests changing manager offers no guarantees. During the 2025-26 season, several clubs that switched coaches continued to struggle. Forest employed three managers during the campaign, Tottenham changed head coach twice, while Chelsea also altered direction before the season ended.

Others, however, did enjoy an immediate uplift. Carrick averaged 2.6 points per game across his first five matches as United boss, while Rosenior collected the same return after taking charge of Chelsea. Rosenior's tenure ultimately proved short-lived, though, with the Blues winning just one of his final eight Premier League matches before he was dismissed.

Research discussed in the Financial Times, external, drawing on findings from Soccernomics by Simon Kuper and Stefan Szymanski, argues that player quality and spending remain stronger predictors of results than managerial changes alone.

Sports consultancy Twenty First Group says coaches often succeed or fail according to the environment they inherit as much as their own abilities.

Since the Premier League began in 1992, only six managers have won the title in their first season in charge of their club.

Mourinho became the first to achieve the feat with Chelsea in 2004-05, before Carlo Ancelotti repeated it with the same club in 2009-10.

Manuel Pellegrini guided Manchester City to the title in his debut campaign in 2013-14, Claudio Ranieri masterminded Leicester City's remarkable triumph in 2015-16, Conte won the league in his first season at Chelsea in 2016-17, and most recently Slot led Liverpool to the championship in his maiden campaign in 2025-26.

With almost half the division beginning the campaign under new leadership, the Premier League enters one of its most unpredictable seasons in recent memory.

England midfielder Jordan Henderson has joined Chelsea on a two-year deal after his contract with Brentford was mutually terminated.

Henderson, 36, captained Liverpool to the Premier League title in 2019-20 and also won the Champions League, FA Cup, League Cup twice, the Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Club World Cup in his time at Anfield.

In 2023 he moved to Saudi Arabian club Al-Ettifaq, before joining Dutch side Ajax in January 2024, and returned to the Premier League with Brentford last summer, making 32 top-flight appearances in 2025-26.

"Given the size of the club, the manager [Xabi Alonso] who I have great admiration for, and the quality of the players, this was a huge opportunity I couldn't turn down," said Henderson.

"For me, it's about giving everything every single day, both on and off the field, to help the players around me and the team as much as possible. I'm very excited to get going."

Henderson came through the ranks at Sunderland and made his Premier League debut for them as a substitute in a 5-0 loss to Chelsea on 1 November, 2008.

Como agree £31m deal to sign Chalobah from Chelsea

Alonso heals Real Madrid scars to lead Chelsea's senior revolution

He earned the first of his 91 England caps in 2010 and has played in seven major international competitions, including the final of the European Championship in 2021 as the Three Lions lost on penalties to Italy.

This summer he became the first Englishman to feature in four different World Cups when he came on as a late substitute in the 2-0 victory over Panama.

However, that would be his only appearance of the tournament as he then suffered a broken arm in freak circumstances.

He fell awkwardly after attempting to jump over the advertising hoardings at the side of the pitch following the 3-2 last-16 victory over Mexico, a match he had not played in. He had also earlier received a booking during the game for criticising a decision by the officials when warming up.

title: How Mumbai Indians takeover has affected MI London & Surrey
description: BBC Sport takes a look at what has changed, what has stayed the same and what the future holds for MI London after investment from Indian Premier League side Mumbai Indians.
fullText:
The name has changed, the colours have changed and much of the conversation around the franchise has changed too.

Investment from Indian Premier League (IPL) side Mumbai Indians into Oval Invincibles led to The Hundred's most successful team rebranding itself as MI London and bringing the multi-billionaire Ambani family's cricket empire to The Oval.

Here, BBC Sport takes a look at what has changed, what has stayed the same and what the future holds for the franchise.

Reliance Industries Limited, chaired by Mukesh Ambani, bought a 49% stake in Oval Invincibles in a deal worth about £60m in January 2025, among the first sale of teams in The Hundred.

However, Surrey chief executive Steve Elworthy said their relationship with India's wealthiest family began long before the bidding process got under way.

"They've been huge supporters of The Hundred for a number of years," the former South Africa cricketer told BBC Sport. "They used to take our boardroom box every August to watch The Hundred when we were still Invincibles."

Early conversations convinced Elworthy and his team they had found the right partner in the Ambanis.

"The first meeting we had, we spent about 45 minutes talking about just cricket," Elworthy said.

At about £120m, MI London are the most valuable of the franchises after their London neighbours - the Lord's-based London Spirit, who were valued at about £300m.

What has changed in The Hundred for 2026?

The Hundred 2026 - schedule and how to follow

For the investors, the attraction must have been obvious.

The Oval is one of the world's most recognisable sporting venues, Invincibles had won five titles across men's and women's competitions and Surrey regularly attracts some of the highest attendances in the county game.

"We do cricket well," Elworthy said. "We've got an incredibly strong membership, incredible attendances across formats and we are based in London. It's a really attractive proposition."

As part of the deal, Invincibles were rebranded MI London, bringing the franchise in line with the rest of the MI stable that includes MI Cape Town, MI Emirates and MI New York.

But Surrey, who remain the major shareholder, were determined not to lose their identity.

Elworthy added: "The beauty of this partnership is that the agreement was signed in late 2025 and we are halfway through our first season together, but we haven't even had to look at the contract once.

"We're only looking to make this a success together."

Not much - at least for the players, according to England all-rounder Will Jacks.

"It felt like a very smooth transition for me, having a foot in both camps," Jacks said, when asked about the team's changed identity.

The 27-year-old came through the ranks at Surrey, was part of Invincibles since its inception and also plays for MI in the IPL.

"The kit's changed obviously and it incorporates the blue and gold of MI but the training kit still has the Invincibles colours, so it is kind of a mix of the two," Jacks said.

"So I think they've done a good job of moulding the two together. But for us players and the coaching staff, everything feels very similar."

Tom Moody, who guided Invincibles to a hat-trick of men's titles as head coach, has been replaced by Kieron Pollard, who previously played in the IPL for MI as well as for their sister teams in Major League Cricket, SA20 and ILT20. Skipper Sam Billings has also left, replaced by Sam Curran.

Mitchell McClenaghan also joined from the MI network as the men's bowling coach but there is still a strong Surrey presence in the coaching staff with Gareth Batty, Jim Troughton and Nic Pothas playing prominent roles.

It's a similar story with the women's side where Lisa Keightley, fresh from coaching MI in the Women's Premier League (WPL), succeeded Jonathan Batty but is joined by Surrey women's head coach Johann Myburgh and Dan Helesfay.

Perhaps the biggest additions from the MI investment have come in the form of commercial expertise and global reach.

"MI have got teams around the world and business around the world, so that's something we've learned from them," Elworthy said.

"The Hundred previously was pretty local. Whereas now, I think we've actually got a global brand here and global partners now. That's a brilliant place to be.

"All other teams MI have around the world, they are the sole owners. But they're a minority shareholder here but we don't behave like that. We behave as a team to do the best for MI London."

Former Australia and England coach Keightley echoed Elworthy's words.

"I know MI have been very mindful that for the first time, they're working with another organisation," Keightley said. "From my experience, both organisations are working really hard to make it successful.

"MI's insight from having so many teams is definitely helpful. I know how passionate the owners are and when they commit to something, they do everything to make sure the team's successful."

For players, it also offers a chance to play for other franchises in the MI network and thereby, grow their game.

"I've been very lucky," Jacks said. "Playing with so many great players and icons of Indian cricket at MI has opened me up to a lot of new things and skills. That experience, you can't buy that."

Keightley added: "If you're a MI London player, there's definitely an opportunity to be involved in WPL. Because you build the relationship, you know what a player can do and they know the environment that they're going into."

Their supporters might still be adjusting to the new name and colours but Surrey and MI are already planning for the future.

One important part of their plans will be turning MI London into a brand that exists year-round rather than for just a few weeks each summer.

"You don't want a competition that everybody only thinks about while it's happening," Elworthy said. "It's our job to make sure there's a cycle all the way through the year."

They also plan to take greater responsibility for areas currently managed by the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB).

Having completed the takeover only months before the start of the season, they have relied on ECB to deliver operational aspects, including ticketing.

But Elworthy said the club are currently considering which services they want to take in-house from 2027.

He said: "We want to control and run all the facets of the team - the delivery of the game, the global expansion and building the brand itself."

On the field though, the ambition remains unchanged. After five titles in as many years, MI London's focus is on producing more silverware-winning teams.

That may happen very soon if their men's team can maintain the form which has seen them reach second in the table after five matches.

description: Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic says defender Charlie Hughes is "far away" from a return from injury and has "no hope" of making the first game of the Premier League season against Manchester United.  Hughes underwent a hernia operation after last season's Wembley success and complained of discomfort when he returned to first-team training this summer. fullText:
Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic says defender Charlie Hughes is "far away" from a return from injury and has "no hope" of making the first game of the Premier League season against Manchester United.

Hughes underwent a hernia operation after last season's Wembley success and complained of discomfort when he returned to first-team training this summer.

Speaking to BBC Radio Humberside about Hughes' rehabilitation, Jakirovic said: "There is a problem and we are trying to solve this problem but it's going very slowly. I think the next two weeks he will still be on an individual programme with the medical team, so no hope for Manchester United.

"Every player, especially from last season who was a main player in our road to Wembley, to the Premier League, has a big role for us."

The Tigers boss was asked if there is a timescale on Hughes' return but replied "too far away."

fullText:
A rebuild was always on the cards on Tyneside this summer, not least in the goalkeeping department.

Leaky Newcastle kept just eight clean sheets in the Premier League last season and conceded 55 goals, 15th overall with only relegated Burnley, West Ham and Wolves plus Leeds and Tottenham below them.

Newcastle's outfield players clearly did not offer enough protection, but goalkeeper Nick Pope made a handful of significant errors leading to goals while Aaron Ramsdale never fully convinced during his loan spell and has since returned to Southampton.

A new number one was therefore a priority and Newcastle have once again looked to the continent.

The club have mainly targeted players aged 20 and under from abroad, having already recruited Jaouen, Sean Steur, Bazoumana Toure and Aladji Bamba, so Lukas Lukas Hornicek will feel like something of an elder statesman in comparison.

But the Czech only made his breakthrough as a regular starter at Braga 18 months ago and will not have much time to prepare for the physicality of the Premier League.

Hornicek's stature will certainly help - he's 6ft 6in tall - and his ability to play out from the back will give this side something different as a new cycle begins under head coach Mattias Jaissle, whose appointment will soon be formally announced.

title: Arsenal Agree to Sell Christian Norgaard to Everton for £7m After Just Seven Premier League Appearances
description:
Arsenal have agreed a deal to sell midfielder Christian Norgaard to Everton for a fee in the region of £7m, ending a stay in north London that lasted little more than a year and produced just seven Premier League appearances. 



 The Athletic’s David Ornstein reported that the two clubs have reached an agreement…
fullText:
Arsenal have agreed a deal to sell midfielder Christian Norgaard to Everton for a fee in the region of £7m, ending a stay in north London that lasted little more than a year and produced just seven Premier League appearances.

The Athletic’s David Ornstein reported that the two clubs have reached an agreement in principle, with Norgaard set to undergo a medical next week ahead of the move being formalised. If completed, it will bring Norgaard back into regular contact with David Moyes, who is entering his second spell in charge at Everton after replacing Sean Dyche.

Norgaard joined Arsenal from Brentford in July 2025 for a fee that could rise to £15m, arriving with a reputation built over six years as the Bees’ defensive midfield anchor and captain. He made 196 appearances for Brentford across his time at the club, taking over the captaincy from Pontus Jansson in 2023 and leading the side 68 times across all competitions.

That standing counted for little once he arrived at the Emirates. Norgaard made just seven Premier League appearances for Arsenal across the season, totalling 101 minutes on the pitch, with only one of those outings coming from the start. His final appearance in Arsenal colours came on May 24 against Crystal Palace, when he played 45 minutes in a 2-1 win. Arsenal’s central midfield had grown crowded well before Norgaard arrived, with Declan Rice established as first choice in the deepest role, Martin Zubimendi brought in from Real Sociedad for a fee that made him one of the club’s most expensive signings, and Mikel Merino also competing for minutes alongside captain Martin Odegaard further forward. Norgaard was squeezed into a squad role behind that group, used mainly to give Arteta the option of resting Rice rather than as a starter in his own right. Arsenal’s decision to cash in on Norgaard with a year still to run on his contract, rather than let him see it out on the fringes of the squad, reflects how little he featured even in a season that ended with the club lifting the Premier League title.

For Everton, the move represents a reunion between Norgaard and Moyes, and a response to a specific gap opening in the dressing room. Club captain Seamus Coleman confirmed earlier this year that his 17-year Everton career will end when his contract expires, closing out a spell in which he made 372 Premier League appearances, an Everton record, and 433 in all competitions after joining from Sligo Rovers in January 2009. Coleman announced the decision in his own words: “After more than 17 years at this great football club, I’ve decided this season will be my last as a player here.” He added a message for supporters: “I want to thank the fans for their unbelievable support. I’ve always tried my best to put Everton Football Club first and you all mean the world to me.” The club has offered Coleman the chance to stay on in a coaching capacity once he decides on the next stage of his career.

Norgaard, who has captained both Brentford and been part of Denmark squads at major tournaments, fits the profile of a player capable of filling that leadership void immediately rather than needing time to grow into it. He has won 41 caps for Denmark and featured in five matches, coming off the bench in both knockout games, as they reached the semi-finals of Euro 2020, giving him exactly the kind of tournament experience Moyes has valued in previous squads he has built.

The move would also mark Norgaard’s fourth new arrival of an Everton rebuild that has been active if unspectacular so far this summer. Moyes has already brought in Hayden Hackney from Middlesbrough in a deal worth an initial £16.5m, made Tyrique George’s loan from Chelsea permanent for a fee above £20m, and signed Merlin Rohl from Freiburg for around £22m to add creativity in the final third. Alongside Coleman, Everton have also let Idrissa Gueye and Tyler Onyango leave on free transfers this summer, meaning the squad Moyes is assembling looks markedly different from the one that finished 13th last season after he returned mid-campaign to steady a club that had flirted with relegation for much of the previous four years.

With Coleman’s exit confirmed, the captaincy itself is also unresolved. Vice-captain James Tarkowski, who joined from Burnley in 2022, has made 128 appearances across all competitions and was named vice-captain in 2023 and has often led the side through Coleman’s injury spells, is widely seen as the leading contender to take over on a permanent basis, with goalkeeper Jordan Pickford and midfielder James Garner also mentioned as possible alternatives, with Garner having started every one of Everton’s 38 Premier League matches last season and led the division for combined tackles, interceptions and key passes along the way. Norgaard would not be walking into a guaranteed armband, but a player with his profile, a former club captain who led Brentford 68 times across all competitions, gives Moyes another senior voice in a dressing room losing one of its longest-serving figures.

Norgaard fits a pattern Moyes has followed throughout his career. In his second spell at West Ham, he built a side that climbed from the relegation zone to winning the UEFA Europa Conference League in 2023, England’s first major trophy for the club in 43 years, largely by recruiting experienced professionals in their mid-to-late twenties rather than chasing potential. Signings like Tomas Soucek and Vladimir Coufal, who arrived together from Slavia Prague for a combined £20m, and defender Craig Dawson became central to that side not through reputation but through consistent, disciplined performances in exactly the kind of holding and defensive roles Norgaard has spent his career playing. Everton fans hoping Norgaard can offer something similar at Goodison Park have that history to point to.

The Norgaard sale is a minor deal set against the scale of Arsenal’s summer activity. The club have already reached an agreement in principle worth around €90m plus bonuses to sign Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes, who has agreed personal terms on a long-term contract, while also being credited with exploring the cost of a move for Real Madrid’s Vinicius Junior, as they look to build on last season’s title win, and selling fringe players like Norgaard for modest fees is a routine part of funding that kind of business. Having brought him in for up to £15m twelve months ago, recovering roughly half that outlay for a player who barely featured represents a pragmatic piece of squad management rather than a setback.

Arsenal’s spending on midfield alone last summer, capped by the Zubimendi deal, meant Norgaard was always likely to be squeezed out once he failed to force his way into Arteta’s first-choice pairing early in the season. Once a midfielder drops that far down the pecking order at a club competing on four fronts, regular football elsewhere becomes the only route back to relevance, and Everton’s £7m offer gives both parties a clean way to move on before the transfer window closes at the start of September.

At 32, Norgaard is unlikely to get many more opportunities to establish himself as a first-choice Premier League midfielder, and a move to Everton offers something Arsenal could not: regular football. His six seasons at Brentford, including the club’s first promotion to the Premier League in 74 years and the survival campaigns that followed it, showed a player who thrives on being trusted with responsibility rather than fighting for scraps of playing time behind more expensive teammates. Moyes has built his sides around experienced, disciplined midfielders in the past, and a player with Norgaard’s positional sense and leadership background suits that approach far better than it suited Arteta’s system built for tempo and press resistance in tighter areas.

Should the medical go smoothly and the transfer complete as expected, Norgaard will arrive at a club searching for exactly the profile his Arsenal spell showed he no longer suited: a captain-type figure who commands a midfield rather than watches most of a season from the bench.

For Arsenal, the deal closes a short and largely forgettable chapter. For Norgaard, it offers a route back to the regular, high-responsibility role he built his reputation on at Brentford, this time in royal blue rather than red and white stripes. Brentford supporters, who watched their former captain leave for a Premier League title winner only a year ago, will notice the irony in seeing him land at Everton rather than fighting for a starting place among the game’s biggest spenders. For Norgaard himself, the move offers something a title medal earned from the bench never could: a manager who wants him on the pitch every week.

title: Newcastle midfielder Bruno Guimaraes set to join Arsenal in £80m deal

fullText:
Newcastle United have reached an agreement with Arsenal over the transfer of midfielder Bruno Guimaraes in a deal worth up to £80 million, ESPN reports.

The Premier League champions have agreed to pay an initial £70m, with a further £10m tied to performance-related bonuses.

The move is expected to be completed once the final formalities are finalised, with Guimaraes set to sign a long-term contract with the North Londoners.

The 29-year-old is also set to undergo a medical on Monday before the transfer is officially announced.

Newcastle have been picked apart this summer, with Guimaraes the latest key figure on the way out of St. James’ Park in what has been a chaotic transfer window for the Magpies.

They had already lost Anthony Gordon to Barcelona and Sandro Tonali to Tottenham Hotspur before manager Eddie Howe’s shocking departure was announced.

With Guimaraes on his way out, Newcastle will need significant investment to rebuild an already depleted squad to boost their chances of competing at the top end of the table this season.

They’ve already sorted out their managerial dilemma, with Matthias Jassle set to replace Howe.

Guimaraes’ desire to join Arsenal reportedly played a huge role in helping the transfer move forward, while Newcastle were prepared to consider offers after missing out on Champions League football.

The Brazilian has been a talismanic figure for Newcastle since joining from Olympique Lyon in January 2022 in a deal worth around £40m.

Over the past few years, he has established himself as one of the team’s leaders and a fan favourite.

He’s also considered one of the best midfielders in the Premier League, which explains why Arsenal were ready to pay a premium fee to secure his services.

Despite missing two months of last season through injury, the Brazilian still finished as Newcastle’s top Premier League goalscorer with nine goals.

He’d become Arsenal’s third signing of the summer, following the arrivals of Greek winger Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge and goalkeeper Illan Meslier, who joined on a free transfer after leaving Leeds United.

title: Arteta coy on Vinicius Jr but says Arsenal very ambitious

fullText:
Mikel Arteta refused to be drawn on speculation linking Arsenal with Real Madrid winger Vinicius Junior but insisted the Premier League champions remain ambitious as they continue to strengthen their squad.

The Arsenal manager was asked about the club’s transfer plans after Saturday’s 4-1 pre-season victory over Girona, where he made it clear that more business is expected before the window closes.

“Well, we are really active, trying to improve and evolve the team. That’s clear,” Arteta said.

“We expect to have movements in the next few weeks, obviously, because we want to get better like anybody else. And you can just see the transfer market and our opponents.

“What we are doing, we won’t sit still, and we are very ambitious in what we want to do.”

Arteta’s comments come amid continued speculation over Vinicius’ future at Real Madrid.

Arteta brushes off Vinicius Jr reports but says Arsenal ‘very ambitious’

Although Arsenal are understood to be monitoring the Brazil international’s contractual situation, Sky Sports News reports that the Spanish giants have no intention of selling the 26-year-old and remain confident he will sign a new long-term deal.

Vinicius has entered the final year of his current contract, prompting interest from several clubs, but Real Madrid continue to regard him as a key part of their long-term project.

Arteta was later asked, in a light-hearted exchange, when Vinicius would be arriving at the Emirates Stadium. The Spaniard responded with a smile before walking away without addressing the question.

Arsenal have made only two senior additions so far this summer, signing Christos Tzolis and Illan Meslier, but Arteta’s latest comments suggest further arrivals remain a priority as the club prepare to defend their Premier League title and challenge on multiple fronts.

While the Arsenal boss offered no indication that a move for Vinicius is imminent, he left little doubt that the club intend to remain active in the market over the coming weeks.

title: What happened to star signings your club never made?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at some star players who were close to moving to the Premier League, only for the deals to fall through.
fullText:
Fans always get excited when the transfer window comes around.

Your team is linked with a big-name signing and you start to dream they could be the ones to lead your club to glory.

Tottenham fans might have felt this way a few years ago when they were strongly linked with a young, prolific striker from Nigeria by the name of Gift Orban.

They had every reason, on paper at least, to be excited.

In the summer of 2023, Orban, then 21, was regarded as one of the hottest prospects in the game.

After scoring 16 goals in 22 games for Norwegian top-flight side Stabaek, he moved to Belgian side Gent and continued his impressive goalscoring record, netting 20 times in 22 matches.

In a wild four-day period in March 2023, he scored seven goals in two matches. He got four in a 6–2 away league win over Zulte Waregem, becoming the first Gent player with a four-goal haul in one game in the 21st Century.

He then followed up with a quick-fire hat-trick in a 4–1 away victory over Istanbul Basaksehir in the Conference League last 16.

That hat-trick was completed within three minutes and 25 seconds, at the time a record in Uefa club competitions.

With England captain Harry Kane set to join Bayern Munich later that summer, Tottenham needed a striker.

Orban was even touted in the BBC Gossip Column as the club's Kane replacement. The headline of a follow-up story read: "Could Orban be a global star?"

However, Spurs, with new boss Ange Postecoglou recently appointed, stalled at the £25m fee and the move collapsed.

In the three years since, Orban has had four clubs, most recently joining newly-promoted Turkish top-flight side Amedspor on loan last week.

He has struggled to regain his form with only three goals for Gent in 2023-24, three for French side Lyon and four for Bundesliga outfit Hoffenheim, although he scored seven times in Serie A on loan at Verona last season.

While his career is yet to reach the heights it once promised, other missed transfer targets have had rather different outcomes...

In January 2009, newly-rich Manchester City were looking to spend a bit of their bulging bank balance to sign Brazilian playmaker Kaka.

AC Milan and Kaka's heads were turned by City's staggering £108m offer, which would have been more than double the world record transfer at the time.

One City fan was so sure the deal would be done that he apparently got the playmaker's name tattooed on his chest., external

However, in the end, the 2007 Ballon d'Or winner decided the timing wasn't right and turned down the chance to move to Manchester.

Kaka did make a world-record move later in 2009, joining Real Madrid for £56m six months later.

He won the Spanish Cup in 2011 and La Liga the following year before one season back at AC Milan.

He then spent three years at Major League Soccer side Orlando City before ending his playing career back in his homeland with Sao Paulo.

In 2004, Bolton Wanderers were flying high, with dreams of Europe.

Manager Sam Allardyce went big, with an enquiry for 32-year-old Brazilian World Cup winner Rivaldo, who had been frozen out at AC Milan.

Rivaldo himself made a statement, saying: "I want the challenge of trying to get Bolton into Europe for the first time in their history. It is an exciting time."

In the end, he had a change of heart and went to Greek side Olympiakos instead, where he stayed for three seasons.

Bolton finished that 2004-05 campaign in sixth - tied on points with Liverpool and just three points off the top four. That earned them a place in Uefa Cup qualifying, and they went on to reach the last 32.

After Olympiakos, Rivaldo had spells with AEK Athens, then in Uzbekistan and Angola before returning to Brazil.

In 1995, Blackburn Rovers had just won the Premier League title and turned down the chance to sign a young French midfielder, Zinedine Zidane from Bordeaux.

Club management urged owner Jack Walker to buy Zidane and France forward Christophe Dugarry, but Walker famously replied: "Why do we need Zidane when we have Tim Sherwood?"

Sherwood had lifted the Premier League trophy a few months earlier and both Zidane and Dugarry had flown to England to talk to the club but no deal was completed.

Zidane and Dugarry went on to win the World Cup with France in 1998 and the European Championship two years later, with Zidane lifting two Italian titles with Juventus and then La Liga and the Champions League with Real Madrid.

Dugarry had spells at AC Milan, Barcelona, Marseille and back at Bordeaux, although he did end his career in England with two seasons at Birmingham City.

In 2005, just off the back of a sensational Champions League win when Liverpool fought back from 3-0 down at half-time against AC Milan before winning on penalties, Steven Gerrard upset the red half of Merseyside. He handed in a transfer request.

Chelsea boss Jose Mourinho was interested in acquiring the England midfielder's services in a potential £32m move, with Gerrard refusing to sign a new contract.

Eventually Gerrard decided to stay with Liverpool, citing "family reasons". Gerrard would go on to make more than 700 appearances for the Reds and guide them to the 2007 Champions League final, although AC Milan would get their revenge.

Ten years later, Mourinho said his failure to sign Gerrard was one of his greatest transfer disappointments.

France striker Kylian Mbappe is the record goalscorer in World Cups, helping his country win the 2018 competition and then scoring a hat-trick in the 2022 final as Les Bleus lost on penalties to Argentina.

However, he could have been a Liverpool player in 2017 as he had talks with the Reds when still at Monaco.

"I talked to Liverpool because it's the favourite club of my mum, my mum loves Liverpool," said Mbappe.

Then-Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp recently revealed how the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family.

However, despite his mother's favourite club being the Reds, Mbappe joined Paris St-Germain, where he won six successive Ligue 1 titles before joining Real Madrid in 2024.

France striker Antoine Griezmann has had a great career, but never played in the Premier League.

But he nearly did, with Fulham making an unlikely £12m bid for him in January 2014 when the Cottagers were fighting to stay in the Premier League.

Fulham enquired about Griezmann to his club Real Sociedad and were quoted a price of £12m. In the end, the west London side spent that figure on Olympiakos striker Kostas Mitroglou, who only played three Premier League matches, scoring no goals, before the Cottagers were relegated.

Mitroglou then had loan spells back at Olympiakos and then Benfica, who he joined permanently in 2016-17.

Griezmann stayed in Spain with nine seasons over two spells at Atletico Madrid and two years at Barcelona. He helped France win the World Cup in 2018.

title: 'Excellent' Liverpool transfer target is now open to exiting his current club
description: Liverpool will be wanting to improve their Premier League standing during the 2026-27 season. The Anfield outfit only mustered up a fifth-place finish last time around which, for a team who were suppo...
fullText:
Liverpool will be wanting to improve their Premier League standing during the 2026-27 season.

The Anfield outfit only mustered up a fifth-place finish last time around which, for a team who were supposed to be defending their title, was a catastrophic result.

The poor performances from most of the Reds' first-team squad led fans to demand that changes were made at Anfield.

And, although the summer window started off pretty well as Liverpool welcomed Jeremy Jacquet and Victor Munoz through the doors, since the Spaniard's arrival, no concrete moves have been made for any other players.

Indeed, rumours about Liverpool preparing a bid for Bradley Barcola have started to emerge but, for now, they're just rumours.

However, one of the Reds' long-linked transfer targets have now had their desire to leave their current club shared which could open the door for Liverpool to swoop in and sign him up.

One of the main areas that Liverpool need to upgrade this summer is their defence.

Virgil van Dijk is now 35 years old and, with Ibrahima Konate now leaving, the Reds' back-line is lacking in depth.

Indeed, Jacquet, Joe Gomez and Giovanni Leoni are all potential options for Liverpool to partner alongside their captain but, with Gomez already out injured and the other two having never played a minute of Premier League football, the Reds' defence is clearly a massive problem.

That's probably one of the many reasons why multiple centre-backs have already been linked with an Anfield switch this summer.

And, even though no move have come to fruition yet, a fresh update from Caught Offside may have just given the green light to Liverpool to try and get a deal over the line for one of their defensive targets.

"Aston Villa centre-back Ezri Konsa is a target for both Arsenal and Liverpool this summer, and he’d be “interested” in a move to the Emirates Stadium," they wrote.

"Liverpool have also been mentioned as potential suitors for Konsa, who seems to be open to leaving Villa Park, even if he’s not currently pushing for the move.

"That leaves Villa in control of the 28-year-old’s situation, so it remains to be seen how things will pan out from here."

Even though Liverpool's centre-backs are certainly an issue, they also have a huge void that they need to fill at right-back.

Not only did they lose Trent Alexander-Arnold at the start of last season but they also signed Jeremie Frimpong to replace him who, after the performances he put in last term, is certainly not a full-back.

And, since Conor Bradley has spent more time on the treatment table than on the pitch recently, he's also unreliable.

This leaves Liverpool with barely any options to choose from at right-back and could force them into using Dominik Szoboszlai or Curtis Jones there instead.

Granted, both of them did fairly well when used as Liverpool's right-back but, if the Reds want to start competing for silverware again, they need natural players in those positions.

That's why Konsa is the perfect signing. The Englishman is a natural centre-back but, as he proved in the 2026 World Cup, he can also be used as a right-back rather effectively.

Indeed, the 'exciting' centre-back is 28 years old so he's a bit older than most of Liverpool's recent targets but, since they've lost so much seniority among their ranks with the departures of Andy Robertson and Mohamed Salah, it feels like some experienced players could be rather useful.

Here's hoping that, even though the Englishman wants to join Arsenal, that Liverpool make their move and get a deal for him over the line.

title: Is building a new stadium a way around spending rules?
description: Spurs only just avoided Premier League relegation last season, but off the pitch they are thriving. So is building a new stadium a good way around spending rules?
fullText:
Tottenham fans will want to put last season behind them.

There was another managerial sacking, a spate of injuries to key players, and a nervy 90 minutes on the final day of the season as the ninth-richest club in the world, external narrowly avoided relegation from the Premier League.

A 17th-place finish for the second year running will be cause for concern, to say the least.

Off the pitch though it's a different story. Tottenham's finances, despite the team's poor form, are looking very rosy indeed. This is largely down to their new stadium and the huge revenues it brings.

So what can other clubs learn from their stadium success story? And is building a new home - or renovating an old one - the best way to balance the books?

We'll get to complying with financial rules in a moment, but first let's start by looking at how much a club like Tottenham are making on matchdays.

"Spurs' matchday income has increased from £45m in 2016-17, the season they left White Hart Lane, to £126m in 2024-25," explains football finance expert Kieran Maguire.

"So you've less than doubled the size of the stadium and yet the matchday revenue is up by two and a half times.

"What Spurs have done is they've created a welcoming environment. So if people are spending an extra 40 to 50 minutes in the stadium itself they're not just spending time - more importantly they're spending money."

Spurs can also host up to 30 non-football events a year at full capacity which is proving to be very beneficial.

Along with major concerts, the club has also hosted NFL games and boxing world title fights - including Anthony Joshua's heavyweight bout with Oleksandr Usyk in 2021. It's also been the venue for rugby union's Saracens hosting Harlequins in the London derby since 2023.

All of this brings in extra commercial revenue - which jumped from £73m in 2016-17 to £277m in 2024-25.

The extra income means the club can then invest 

This summer the Premier League is replacing its profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) with a new financial framework centred on squad-cost ratio (SCR) and sustainability and systemic resilience (SSR).

Put simply, SCR is designed to cap a club's total spending on its playing squad as a direct percentage of its overall revenue.

Club costs like player wages, transfer amortisation - spreading a transfer fee across the length of a player's contract for accounting purposes - and agent fees all get taken into account.

Crucially though, stadium infrastructure costs are not included in the SCR calculation.

"In the case of Spurs, their infrastructure costs are around £70m a year - but those are excluded." says Maguire. "Any money that you invest in stadiums is completely ring-fenced and excluded from your ability to invest in players.

"There's a separate issue in that stadiums do cost a lot of money. But Spurs borrowed from banks at spectacularly cheap interest rates."

In other words, for Spurs the pluses of building a new expensive stadium far outweigh the negatives, at least from a financial perspective.

"In order to be competitive, you need to have a significant increase in matchday income," says Maguire.

"You could only do that from either increasing prices, which isn't going to go down well, or increasing the size of the stadium with a greater proportion of the tickets going to the non-season ticket fanbase."

Like Tottenham, Everton and West Ham have also moved to new stadiums - which while financially attractive in the long-term, hasn't always gone down well with fans.

Other Premier League clubs are looking at their options. Should they stay or go?

Renovation is the cheaper route, but the problem then is where do the team play if they have to move out while building takes place?

The obvious barrier to moving to a new stadium is the huge cost - but there's also the concern from fans that they'll lose something by leaving their historical home.

It is clear Sir Jim Ratcliffe wants a new stadium to be the statement around his involvement at Manchester United.

Yet it is equally clear a new build, with a 100,000 capacity and a significant number of corporate areas, would generate far more than United get on a matchday now, which will help drive revenues and improve the senior squad.

There are other financial aspects though, which few will consider in the bigger picture.

The initial plans unveiled by Ratcliffe in March 2025 featured a huge canopy. That in itself will be costly, but in theory the overhang and what is underneath it will be in United's footprint - and the club will be responsible for it. Will the expense be worth the 'look'?

Construction could - in part - take place off site and be shipped in if club officials are to be believed. That is likely to cost less than doing all the work in Old Trafford.

And then having a new build where it is, down the road from their current ground, deals with the potentially thorny problem about where United would play if Old Trafford was closed for a period.

None of Manchester City, Liverpool or Everton's grounds are ideal from a security perspective. All have a lower capacity than Old Trafford and all would cost a lot to hire, even if it was desirable.

United's current plans mean they can simply move from one stadium to another.

For Newcastle, a club which this summer has effectively had to sell some of its best players in order to stay within the financial rules, the argument over moving to a new purpose-built stadium is compelling.

"For the 2024-25 season Newcastle's matchday income was £52m. Manchester United's was £160m, Arsenal's £154m, Spurs' was £126m.

"If you're £100m behind your competitors, the only way to address that is either to be super smart or to charge more money for the product.

"How can Newcastle increase the yield per fan and still be loyal to the Gallowgate hardcore? You need to be able to offer a different product and St James' Park wasn't built for a corporate audience."

Will the fans back a move though?

Newcastle supporter Charlotte Robson has mixed feelings.

"I think we can host gigs at St James' Park but probably not on the scale of Spurs or West Ham's London Stadium.

"I don't think it would be stupid to move from the ground but I think there is so much identity for Newcastle fans who are attached to St James' Park that it would break a lot of hearts to move the ground in any significant way."

Along with increased matchday revenue, clubs weighing up whether to move will also hope to make more commercial revenue - but Maguire is cautious.

"Spurs have got the advantage that they're in London - a huge tourist trap. They are also a club with a global fanbase, so it works there.

"Is that going to work elsewhere in the country where you've got a more localised fanbase and where there is resistance to putting up prices for tickets? Then it becomes more challenging.

"We have seen a substantial increase in the costs of putting stadiums together, but there still seems to be an appetite for it."

title: The Premier League clubs fighting a World Cup hangover
description: Which Premier League clubs have carried the biggest World Cup workload?
fullText:
The Premier League season begins on 21 August - just 33 days after the World Cup final.

For some clubs, that leaves barely enough time to welcome players back from the mandatory three-week post-tournament break required under Fifa regulations, let alone integrate them into pre-season preparations.

Four Tottenham players were still involved on the final weekend of the tournament and may have little more than a week of training before the new campaign starts. Chelsea too were significantly affected.

And Manchester City and Arsenal have their own concerns after seeing more players than any other Premier League club reach the latter stages of the competition.

The World Cup may be over, but its impact on the Premier League is only just beginning.

Tottenham are among the clubs whose pre-season preparations have been most significantly impacted.

Cristian Romero and new signing Marcos Senesi reached the final with Argentina, while Pedro Porro helped Spain lift the trophy. Djed Spence remained with England until the third-place play-off on 18 July.

Assuming players take the minimum three weeks off under Fifa guidelines, the players who reached the final would not return until 9 August, while Spence's earliest return date would be 8 August.

That leaves them with around two weeks to reintegrate before their Premier League season begins at Brentford on 22 August.

However, Spurs confirmed that Senesi - who made two World Cup appearances after being a late call-up for Argentina - was at the club's training ground for the first time on Thursday for pre-season testing.

For managers, the challenge is not simply the absence itself. Players returning so late miss much of pre-season's tactical work, conditioning sessions and friendly matches, creating a difficult balancing act between preparation and recovery.

Manchester City and Arsenal, meanwhile, had the greatest concentration of players making deep runs into the competition.

City's World Cup contingent featured for several of the tournament's leading nations.

Rodri helped Spain win their second men's World Cup after playing 726 minutes, while Marc Guehi and Elliot Anderson helped England reach the final weekend.

Nico O'Reilly featured in England's semi-final run, while Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku both reached the quarter-finals.

Arsenal's numbers were similarly striking.

Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka remained involved until England's 6-4 victory over France in the third-place play-off, while Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino reached the final with Spain.

William Saliba helped France reach the third-place play-off, although he was subsequently injured and did not feature again. Noni Madueke was part of England's run to the final weekend but did not play beyond the quarter-finals, while Martin Odegaard captained Norway to the quarter-finals.

The workload concerns are already being felt. City's Rodri recently had back surgery and is expected to miss a "short period" at the start of the season, while Saliba avoided surgery, but Arsenal have confirmed he will be sidelined for an "extended period" because of a back issue.

Even though neither setback can be attributed solely to the World Cup, both underline the physical demands being placed on players in an increasingly crowded football calendar.

Those clubs are likely to begin the campaign without having enjoyed a full pre-season with several key players.

The World Cup's biggest workload belonged to Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who played all 810 minutes of Argentina's run to the final.

Liverpool midfielder Alexis Mac Allister ranked second among Premier League players with 749 minutes, while Spain midfielder Rodri was third on 726.

Several players effectively completed the equivalent of eight full matches during the tournament.

Goalkeepers naturally face different physical demands from outfield players, but the figures underline the extent of Premier League involvement throughout the competition.

With the players entitled to a minimum three-week break under Fifa regulations, for those involved in the final on 19 July - including Rodri, Porro, Zubimendi, Mac Allister, Enzo Fernandez, Emiliano Martinez and Lisandro Martinez - the earliest return date is 9 August.

Players who featured in England's third-place play-off will return a day earlier.

That leaves clubs with roughly 12 days to reintegrate some of their most important players before competitive football begins.

The concerns extend beyond this summer's World Cup.

Many of football's leading players have now experienced three consecutive summers of major tournaments, following Euro 2024 and Copa America, then last year's expanded Club World Cup and now the World Cup.

One of those players is Rodri, who warned in 2024 that footballers were "close" to striking because of workload concerns.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta and Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca have also voiced concerns about the demands being placed on elite players and the growing number of matches in the calendar.

The growing injury list during the World Cup provided another reminder of those concerns.

Aston Villa midfielder Amadou Onana suffered a serious knee injury while representing Belgium, while Manchester United and Uruguay defensive midfielder Manuel Ugarte saw his tournament cut short by injury. Reece James also had his minutes carefully managed by England as he continued his recovery from a hamstring problem.

For clubs such as Tottenham, Arsenal, Manchester City and Chelsea, the challenge is now immediate.

The World Cup has concluded. The countdown to the Premier League season is under way.

But for some players, recovery comes first, and the race to be ready for opening weekend has only just begun.

title: 22 needed off 6: Ex-CSK star Vijay Shankar's batting ends in wicket-maiden as Dilshan Madushanka seals last-over win in LPL
description: The Lanka Premier League continues to be one of the most thrilling T20 leagues as Vijay Shankar's shocking batting in the final over ends with a wicket-maiden and defeat.
fullText:
22 needed off 6: Ex-CSK star Vijay Shankar's batting ends in wicket-maiden as Dilshan Madushanka seals last-over win in LPL originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Dilshan Madushanka bowled a final-over wicket maiden to seal Jaffna Kings' win in LPL 2026.

Kandy Royals needed 22 off the last six balls with one recognised batter left.

Former CSK star Vijay Shankar was dismissed off the final delivery as Kandy fell 21 short.

The Lanka Premier League served up a gripping finish in Pallekele on Thursday, with a title contender's chase collapsing at the last hurdle. What had been a high-scoring contest between Jaffna Kings and Kandy Royals came down to a single, unforgettable over from a Sri Lanka international.

Batting first after being invited to do so, Jaffna posted an imposing 221/6, built on brisk contributions through their order. As reported by NDTV, Kamil Mishara top-scored with 49 while Chamindu Wickramasinghe provided late impetus with 43 off just 15 balls, setting Kandy a daunting target.

Kandy Royals mounted a spirited response but ultimately fell short, bowled out for 200 to lose by 21 runs. The chase never quite kept pace with the rate, and the equation grew steeper as wickets tumbled around a series of promising starts.

MORE: Jamie George and Owen Farrell to take on Somerset cricket stars in charity T20 match

The decisive drama unfolded in the 20th over, with Kandy requiring 22 runs from six balls and clinging to their last recognised batter. Left-arm quick Dilshan Madushanka was handed the ball against former India batter Vijay Shankar, and he responded with a spell of ruthless precision.

According to ESPNcricinfo's commentary, Madushanka speared in a mix of slower off-cutters and yorkers that left Shankar swinging in vain. Five successive dot balls followed, the batter unable to make clean contact, before Madushanka rounded off the wicket-maiden by dismissing Shankar off the final delivery to seal victory in style.

Shankar, who had earlier fought to 25 off 21 balls, could only pull the last ball to deep backward square leg, ending both the innings and Kandy's hopes. The win lifted Jaffna to the top of the points table.

MORE: 'Simply no match for him': Amir names Virat as the toughest to bowl

The foundation for Jaffna's defence was laid long before the final over. As reported by NDTV, Dunith Wellalage swung the contest firmly in the Kings' favour with an outstanding spell of 3/11, choking Kandy's momentum through the middle overs.

He found able support across the attack. Shakib Al Hasan chipped in with important wickets, while Kandy's brightest resistance came from Pawan Sandesh, whose quick-fire 48 from 21 deliveries briefly threatened before the asking rate spiralled beyond their reach.

For Kandy, two wickets apiece from Wanindu Hasaranga and Moeen Ali had kept Jaffna's total within reach, but the batting could not finish the job. Jaffna Kings will now face Dambulla Sixers on Sunday in their final league fixture.

MORE: Sammy vs Joseph: What happened as WI pacer drops 'not representing Sammy' bombshell

The margin of 21 runs and the theatre of the last over should not disguise what was, in truth, a comfortable Jaffna win. Kandy's chase flickered without ever genuinely threatening, and needing 22 off the final six with one wicket standing was less a nail-biter than a formality dressed up as tension.

The lasting image, though, belongs to Madushanka, whose ice-cold execution under the lights offered a reminder of his international pedigree. For Shankar and Kandy, it was a deflating way to surrender a contest, their playoff hopes fraying further with each dot ball of an over they would want to forget.

title: England's Stones joins Inter Milan on free transfer
description: England centre-back John Stones has joined Inter Milan on a free transfer after spending 10 years with Manchester City, the Italian champions announced on Thursday.Stones was a key player for Manchester City during their golden era under former manager Pep Guardiola, winning six Premier League titles, three FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League crown with the club.
fullText:
England centre-back John Stones has joined Inter Milan on a free transfer after spending 10 years with Manchester City, the Italian champions announced on Thursday.

The 32-year-old left City when his contract expired at the end of last month, while playing for England at the World Cup where he helped them to a third-placed finish.

Stones has signed a two-year deal with Inter, a club statement said.

He played five times for England at the recent World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada, making his 94th international appearance in the semi-final loss to Argentina.

Stones was a key player for Manchester City during their golden era under former manager Pep Guardiola, winning six Premier League titles, three FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League crown with the club.

His final few seasons at the Etihad Stadium, though, were hit by injuries, and he only made nine Premier League appearances last term.

Stones could make his Inter debut when they start their Scudetto defence against Monza at the San Siro on August 22.

title: Premier League clubs agree EFL funding proposal
description: Premier League clubs agreed a funding proposal that they will put to the EFL over the next few days.
fullText:
An end is finally in sight to the long-running funding dispute between the Premier League and the English Football League.

The Premier League confirmed its 20 clubs have "unanimously voted" to approve a proposal for a "new strategic partnership", which will be put to the EFL for its members to vote on in the next few days.

No figure has been put on the deal, which is due to last 10 years, with both sides keen not to debate the issue in public.

The Premier League says the proposal is fully funded. It is expected to come through a transfer levy.

"The Premier League already has long-term funding commitments to invest a record £1.6billion every three years into the wider game and communities," said the Premier League.

"The Premier League remains committed to finding a football-led solution and looks forward to continuing discussions with the EFL on progressing this proposal."

'Clock ticking' on financial stand-off - regulator

The funding row has been rumbling on since a fan-led review in 2021, which was commissioned by the government following a number of crises in the sport, including the failed European Super League project and the collapse of Bury FC.

On a number of occasions, it has seemed a deal was close. In March 2024, the Premier League was warned by government officials that if it and the EFL failed to agree a deal, one would be imposed on them.

On Tuesday, representatives of the Premier League, the EFL and the new Independent Regulator met to discuss the outline of a deal.

"The EFL notes the Premier League's position following its meeting with clubs earlier today, and now looks forward to receiving its formal proposal for consideration," said the EFL.

"This follows constructive discussions involving the EFL, Premier League and Independent Football Regulator over recent months.

"The EFL Board will then review the full detail of the proposal, including its potential benefits, implications and alignment with the long-term interests of our 72 clubs, ahead of further dialogue with the Premier League.

"The proposal will then be discussed in detail with our member clubs to determine next steps."

Resistance within the Premier League simply to hand over money was based on a number of factors, including the basic reality they would providing funds to clubs trying to replace them.

In other instances, specifically Stoke City, EFL clubs have owners richer than some in the Premier League.
